sections.title: What Residents Are Already Paying For

items.title: November 2025 E-SPLOST
items.detail: Voters approved the one-cent education sales tax: 3,263 Yes (76.15%) and 1,022 No. The authorization allows up to $45 million of collections for no more than 20 quarters and up to $50 million of general-obligation bonds.

items.title: Athletic, technology and school capital
items.detail: The authorized list includes an Athletic and Sports Complex plus devices, servers, cabling, wireless access points, VoIP, software and instructional/safety systems. Major private investment should first identify the funded scope and remaining gaps rather than duplicate approved assets.

items.title: Existing public-capital programs
items.detail: The FY2024 school audit carries the prior $30 million E-SPLOST program through June 2027, and the county FY2024–2025 budget included $1.354 million of T-SPLOST resources. Authorization and budget availability do not prove implementation status.

sections.title: What a Data Center Could Help Solve
sections.intro: Developer-required infrastructure, temporary construction jobs and one-time gifts without operating plans do not count here as durable community benefit.

items.title: Sustain the people who make youth facilities work
items.detail: Link: school capital plus youth-pathway evidence. Potential response: shared-use agreements, transport, qualified instructors, safeguarding, maintenance and recurring program support—not another unfunded building.

items.title: Make technical pathways portable
items.detail: Link: SGTC, GSW, Ignite and existing computing instruction. Potential response: instructor capacity, apprenticeships, credential equipment and community-owned labs whose skills serve multiple employers.

items.title: Leave the public utility stronger
items.detail: Link: audited enterprise finances and planned water capital. Potential response: pay full attributable project costs and separately negotiate reusable system improvements, household-resilience measures and transparent long-term maintenance funding.

items.title: Activate existing buildings and downtown investment
items.detail: Link: downtown streetscape funding and unresolved former Americus High reuse. Potential response: fund due diligence and reuse only after title, condition, environmental, ownership and operating questions are resolved.

items.title: Diversify beyond one major project
items.detail: Link: prepared industrial land, institutions and manufacturing activity. Potential response: a community-controlled endowment, supplier development and multi-employer recruitment with public outcome reporting.

items.title: Consistent personnel-cost logic
items.detail: Direct salary expense controls when reported; neither school audit reports it. Both auditor reports say MD&A was omitted, and neither supplies an object-level salary/benefit expenditure schedule. Covered payroll is therefore displayed only as a corroborating basis, with TRS, PSERS and OPEB schedules kept separate because their populations and measurement periods differ. Salaries-and-benefits-payable balances are liabilities and are not treated as annual expense.

items.title: What the percentages mean
items.detail: Instruction and administration shares use total governmental-fund expenditures as the denominator. Administration combines general, school and business administration. Pension and OPEB percentages use government-wide expenses and are GASB actuarial accounting measures, not cash benefit spending or a substitute for actual personnel expense. Covered-payroll benchmark percentages use total governmental-fund expenditures and are not salary-expense percentages.

items.title: Operating sustainability test
items.detail: A one-time lab or building grant does not prove either LEA can sustain specialized teachers, transportation, maintenance, subscriptions and equipment refresh for decades. Any new program needs a recurring operating plan.

items.title: Furlow oversight
items.detail: SCSC's 2024–25 framework rated Furlow 100 on fiscal viability and 70 on financial management/oversight, producing an overall Approaches Standards result. Its current charter contract runs 2025–2030.

items.title: Four-phase campus
items.detail: The signed July 1, 2026 agreement covers about 102 acres and defines full buildout as at least approximately 400,000 square feet: an innovation center, logistics building, substation and four data-center buildings. Phase 1 is due by December 2029 and phases 2–4 by December 2033.

items.title: Investment and operations
items.detail: Liberty committed to approximately $1B–$5B of investment and at least 30 years of continuous operation, with annual reporting in years 2–5 and contractual performance protections.

items.title: Land transaction
items.detail: The PDA agreed to convey property with an acknowledged $469,000 fair value for $1, subject to performance and repurchase provisions. The public agreement is not itself a complete tax-abatement, PILOT or bond record.

items.title: Tenant and operating model
items.detail: No primary record reviewed identifies Meta, Google, OpenAI or another hyperscaler. Hyperscale, AI/HPC, enterprise, colocation and multi-tenant use remain possibilities only.

items.title: Rendering is conceptual
items.detail: The preliminary draft rendering illustrates phasing, roads, buildings, parking and a switchyard, but it is not an engineered civil plan or proof of fit on developable uplands.

items.title: Jobs Attribution Test
items.detail: For every counted job, disclose employer, occupation, work location, direct/contract/affiliate status, duration, full-time status, permanence, incentive treatment and whether it appears in another count.

items.title: Municipal water and sewer requirement
items.detail: The agreement prohibits private wells and requires application for City water and sewer service. Liberty is responsible for project infrastructure unless the City determines otherwise.

items.title: Existing public water priority
items.detail: Georgia's FY2025 DWSRF list reports a $12M Americus drinking-water project intended to serve more than 200 customers from a contaminated private system.

items.title: Community-benefit test
items.detail: Before commitments are treated as beneficial, a utility professional should model capacity, upgrades, capital responsibility, debt, reserves, operating cost, rate allocation and potential effects on existing customers. Do not promise lower rates.

items.title: Southwest Georgia network context
items.detail: Existing research places Americus within a regional transmission network involving the North Americus–Palmyra corridor, Crisp public power, Ellaville municipal service, Sumter EMC and Georgia's Integrated Transmission System. This context does not establish deliverable project capacity.

items.title: Project-specific power remains unknown
items.detail: The bounded search found no Liberty will-serve letter, megawatt schedule, source substation, firm-service agreement, transmission study, upgrade plan or cost-allocation record. The rendering's substation symbol is not capacity evidence.

items.title: Regional generation is not project supply
items.detail: Previously identified solar/storage interconnection activity near the Americus corridor is regional context only and must not be presented as serving Liberty.

sections.title: Environmental & Site Constraints
sections.kicker: Delineation is not a final permit

items.title: Wetlands and streams
items.detail: Terracon delineated approximately 61.47 wetland acres—59.16% of the approximately 103.91-acre study area—plus about 1,862 linear feet of perennial stream and 69 feet of ephemeral stream.

items.title: Jurisdiction and permitting
items.detail: Terracon believed jurisdictional waters were present, but only the U.S. Army Corps can make a final jurisdictional determination. Impacts may require Section 404 authorization and mitigation.

items.title: Source-quality conflict
items.detail: The report title, addressee, maps and site description identify Americus, but one sentence says the field survey covered a project area in Unadilla. This apparent template/location error requires confirmation with Terracon or the commissioning authority.

items.title: Civil reconciliation
items.detail: No public final plan reviewed reconciles wetland avoidance, fill, mitigation, stormwater, roads, parking, buildings and substation footprints by phase.

items.title: Cooling restriction
items.detail: The agreement prohibits open-loop and once-through cooling and requires closed-loop or other technology intended to minimize water consumption.

items.title: Actual cooling architecture
items.detail: Closed-loop chilled water, dry cooling, hybrid cooling, direct-to-chip liquid cooling and immersion are industry examples—not evidence of Liberty's selected system.

items.title: Sustainable capacity
items.detail: Available utility service is not the same as environmentally and politically sustainable capacity. Peak-day demand, wastewater return, drought response and competing residential/agricultural needs need professional review.

items.title: Current classification: Proposed / under review
items.detail: The local folder contains an unsigned 18-month joint-resolution draft with blank adoption date and signatures. The bounded official search did not locate an adopted City or County data-center-specific ordinance or adopted moratorium.

items.title: Controls to evaluate
items.detail: Definitions, zoning districts, special-use review, setbacks, buffers, low-frequency noise, lighting, generators, emissions, cooling/water, wastewater, BESS/fire, transmission, construction traffic, wetlands, decommissioning, financial assurance, expansion and annual reporting all need a verified code crosswalk.

items.title: Process recommendation
items.detail: Publish plain-language agreements and technical summaries; hold public technical briefings and ordinance workshops; separate developer claims from binding obligations; and disclose verified community-benefit commitments.

items.title: Community concern
items.detail: Community sources report concern about the timing, completeness and transparency of public communication surrounding the project and are organizing informational meetings and a moratorium petition.

items.title: What is not established
items.detail: The reviewed material does not prove intentional concealment, legal notice failure, unanimous opposition or community consent. Meeting notices, votes, correspondence and open-records responses require record-by-record review.

items.title: Readiness implication
items.detail: Unresolved communication and ordinance questions can create execution risk even when technical feasibility later proves adequate.

items.title: Development pathway
items.detail: A practical pathway is belonging → technology exposure → technology literacy → creation → credentials → paid work. Programming may include arts, recreation, robotics, maker work, electronics, coding, AI creation and mentoring.

items.title: Middle-school focus
items.detail: Ages approximately 11–15 merit dedicated engagement, safe access, transportation and qualified staffing. This is youth development—not marketing to children and not a claim that technology solves structural social issues.

items.title: Operating plan first
items.detail: Any facility proposal must fund instructors, safeguarding, transportation, food, insurance, utilities, maintenance, subscriptions and equipment replacement beyond the opening grant.

items.title: Former high school status
items.detail: The bounded search found media evidence of continued school athletic use and a future community-center concept, but did not establish current title ownership, legal availability or building condition. The asset cannot yet be promised for Furlow or a youth hub.

items.title: Ownership test
items.detail: For each proposed major benefit, ask who owns it after Liberty leaves. Prefer a school system, SGTC, municipality, public authority or protected community trust over a developer-controlled facility behind a secure campus.

items.title: One community-controlled fund
items.detail: Study a Sumter Community Resilience & Opportunity Endowment with restricted Energy Resilience, Youth & Education, Workforce, and Emergency/Community Infrastructure accounts. Liberty funds; the community owns; successor obligations follow the asset.

items.title: Illustrative scale
items.detail: A purely illustrative $500,000–$1,000,000 per approved MW would equal $50M–$100M at 100 MW, plus a possible per-MWh operating contribution and measurable-impact adders. Liberty MW is unknown, so this is not a project valuation or commitment.

items.title: Energy-choice design
items.detail: Potential resident options include rooftop efficiency/solar/storage, community subscription/storage, resilience-only upgrades, or an equivalent lawful benefit. Measure energy-burden reduction rather than panel count.

sections.title: Southwest Georgia Technology Hub
sections.kicker: The anchor should attract the next employer

items.title: Potential cluster
items.detail: A long-term strategy could connect SGTC, GSW, NanoPV, utilities, agriculture, fiber, industrial parks and digital infrastructure to recruit 30–100-person firms in controls, cybersecurity, GIS, drones, ag-tech, robotics, energy systems, networking and cooling technology.

items.title: Landing space gap
items.detail: No evidence reviewed establishes a community-owned, fiber-ready accelerator with flexible offices, secure networking, lab/maker space and shared access to SGTC/GSW. Identify or designate such space before claiming a hub exists.

items.title: Regional—not merged
items.detail: Leslie may be studied as a complementary drone, logistics and ag-tech node while Americus anchors education, computing, manufacturing and energy. Formal collaboration is not established.

items.title: A stronger public utility
items.detail: Reusable infrastructure, reserves and transparent cost allocation should remain with the public system; project-only facilities and uncompensated operating burdens should not be counted as community benefit.

items.title: Sustained youth and school capacity
items.detail: Facilities should retain public access, qualified staff, transport, maintenance and technology replacement funding after initial construction and independent of the developer's brand.

items.title: Portable skills and multiple employers
items.detail: Credentials, instructors, laboratories and apprenticeships should prepare residents for data infrastructure, manufacturing, health care and other employers—not a single tenant's proprietary needs.

items.title: Restored assets under durable local control
items.detail: Any reused downtown or school property should have settled title, safe occupancy, a responsible owner and a funded operating plan that survives project ownership changes.

items.title: Governance and community-controlled capital
items.detail: Public reporting capacity and protected endowment principal should remain locally accountable, with spending rules, audits and conflict safeguards independent of one company.

sections.title: 30-Year Community Legacy
sections.kicker: What remains after the ribbon cutting

items.title: Durable ownership
items.detail: Community-owned utility improvements, educational capacity, rehabilitated public assets and protected endowment principal should remain useful if the operator, tenant or technology changes.

items.title: Recurring operations
items.detail: A 30-year project benefit should be tested against 30-year staffing, maintenance, technology refresh, battery replacement, transportation, insurance and program costs.

items.title: Diversification
items.detail: Success is not dependence on one employer; it is the community's stronger ability to retain talent and attract multiple additional employers.

items.title: Technical proof
items.detail: Establish electric service, phased load, transmission impacts, water/wastewater capacity, final cooling and a buildable civil plan before describing the project as technically feasible.

items.title: Governance proof
items.detail: Establish the applicable ordinance, public process, permitting sequence, incentive structure, annual reporting and enforceable community-benefit obligations.

items.title: Institutional proof
items.detail: Obtain board-approved MOUs and sustainable operating budgets before counting education, workforce, youth or shared-use concepts as project benefits.

items.title: Power and delivery
items.detail: Liberty MW by phase; serving utility; will-serve; service dates; source substation; transformer/transmission upgrades; study results; firm/interruptible terms; cost responsibility; ramp, harmonics and curtailment requirements.

items.title: Environment and water
items.detail: Final civil site plan; Corps JD; Section 404 application/permit; mitigation; stormwater; floodplain; developable acreage; phase impacts; cooling design; peak water and wastewater profile.

items.title: Jobs and partnerships
items.detail: Job occupations and employers; education MOUs; instructor/program commitments; internships; double-counting safeguards; workforce reporting.

items.title: Finance and governance
items.detail: Tax abatement/PILOT/bond structure; PDA standalone financials; resolution of City FY2024 audit findings and current enterprise capacity study; adopted ordinance and moratorium status; E-SPLOST implementation schedules; binding community-benefit agreement.

items.title: Reuse
items.detail: Former Americus High title owner, legal availability, structural/environmental condition, fields/courts inventory and rehabilitation/operating cost.
